narrative:
The model estimates an 84% probability that you will leave your job. Because that is high, the promotion decision was to deny it: the organization is treating you as a strong retention risk rather than as an employee likely to stay and grow here. This prediction is based on job-related information, not your gender, age, or health.

Three factors drove it most. The strongest was that you reported having other job opportunities. Among employees predicted to stay, about 77% had no such opportunities, so your situation stands out and pushed the prediction strongly toward leaving. Second was your overall experience band of 6–10 years. Although about 35% of stay-predicted employees are in that band, in your combination of circumstances it still increased the leaving risk. Third was working in a sector classified as other. Most stay-predicted employees work in medical or education, and only about 22% are in other sectors, so this also nudged the prediction toward leaving. All three top factors pushed in the same direction: toward leaving, not staying.

Next, you and your manager should discuss why other opportunities feel attractive, what career path and promotion timeline are realistic, and what retention steps—such as clearer advancement, recognition, or rewards—could make staying more compelling. The organization should treat this as a signal to review your engagement and development rather than as a final judgment about your value.
